title: Data and vectors
why: Retrieval is a data problem. Add Postgres, embeddings and vector search, and you have the storage layer for every RAG system.
outcomes: Run similarity search with pgvector and an index
Design a chunks table that supports filtering and citation
lessons: Run Postgres through Docker or Supabase; connect with psycopg
What embeddings are; generate them with an API or a local model
pgvector: store vectors, query by cosine distance, add an HNSW index
Design a chunks table: id, document_id, text, embedding, source, page, created_at
Combine vector search with SQL filters by source and date
resources: Learn PostgreSQL: Full Course for Beginners
Tables, queries and joins in Postgres, typed along with you.
Vector Databases: from Embeddings to Applications
Under an hour on embeddings, similarity search and hybrid search, with notebooks.
method: Write the SQL first, then add vectors. Run 20 questions through keyword search and vector search side by side, and write down where each wins.
build: A script that embeds 100 documents into pgvector and returns the five most similar passages for a question, with sources.

quiz.q: Which join returns only rows that match in both tables?
quiz.e: INNER JOIN keeps matches only; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table.

o: A compressed copy of the text
A list of numbers that represents meaning, so similar texts sit close together
quiz.e: Embeddings map text into vectors where distance tracks semantic similarity.
<=> is cosine distance; <-> is Euclidean distance.

quiz.q: Why add an HNSW index on the vector column?
o: To find approximate nearest neighbours fast at scale
quiz.e: HNSW trades a little exactness for large speed gains on big tables.

quiz.q: Why store source and page with each chunk?
o: So you can filter results and cite where an answer came from
quiz.e: Metadata powers filtering and the citations that make answers trustworthy.
